speechtext:
The hon. member for
Antigonish-Guysborough has asked the reason for the resolution before us. I believe it is self-explanatory. It is intended to be the basis of a bill which will have for its object the continuance for one more year of the salary deductions of last year. With one exception the bill, if it is approved by the house, will be precisely the same as that of last year. The only difference is that it will contain a clause making it clear that the indemnity for the present session of parliament will be taxable for income tax purposes
in the taxation period of 1933. The object of that provision will be readily apparent to hon. members. Otherwise an injustice would arise in the case of any members whose indemnities would be increased out of proper proportion to the amount of income tax which they ought properly to pay in any one income tax period.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONTINUATION OF DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT FROM INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, for the reasons I gave last year, I do not wish to be taken as in any way approving the passing of this resolution. At this stage it is not my intention to repeat my former arguments. The statements I made to the house last year will be made even more forcibly again this year. I am absolutely and irrevocably opposed to the adoption of this measure and any bill which miay be founded upon it, or any bill which may be founded upon a similar resolution. I reserve mly right to protest on every occasion the matter may be brought before the house, namely when the bill may be introduced, and when it appears for second reading.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONTINUATION OF DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT FROM INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to make some observations concerning the resolution now before us. Last year and the year before there were no very strong protests against the reductions, because we wanted to give the government a chance. However during the first part of this session hon. members of the opposition have proved that the-high tariff policy of the government has: caused the external trade of our country to decrease. We maintain that the worries obtaining in many homes may be traced directly to the salary cuts and that they affect internal trade. The resolution before us constitutes one of the silly policies inaugurated by the provincial government of Ontario. Without inquiry this government has followed the example set by the Ontario legislature. I should like to offer a few suggestions before the government make any definite decision in this matter; there is still time for them to change their minds.
First of all, there are eight vacancies in the Senate. The government have a majority in the Senate, and they are sure to carry their legislation through that body, whenever they think fit. What is the necessity of spending [DOT]S32.000 per annum in order to fill those vacancies? The government could wait until a time immediately preceding the next general elections, whether they take place this year or next. If they take place this year the government would save $32,000 and if next year; $64,000. In this particular I offer another-suggestion to the leader of the government:
Salary Deduction Act

There might be some applications for senator-ships. Quite so. I suggest the government should notify all the applicants that only one application should be sent, and when a second application is sent, the government should take the stand that the applicant would not get the job. They should post notices, or in some other way notify those who want to be appointed to the Senate that if they come twice to get the appointment they will get nothing. They should be notified that if a man, after having applied to the Senate, sends his friend or any one else, or canvasses any ministers of the crown, he will be sure not to get the job. This is a very practical and timely suggestion, and will give the Prime Minister and other members of the government a chance to enjoy more peace and rest. I suggest that before cutting salaries the decision should be made that no other Senator should be appointed before the next general election.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONTINUATION OF DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT FROM INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I thank hon. members very much for carrying my first suggestion and I hope anything further I have to say will be received in the same spirit. In our confederation there are nine provinces. Citizens of the province of Ontario as well as those of the province of Quebec are interested in the welfare of the seven other provinces of our dominion, from sea to sea-but not farther than that. We are not interested in the situation obtaining in Newfoundland. What happens in Newfoundland is of no particular interest to us, since it took a slice from Labrador, thanks to the indulgence or diplomacy of the Privy Council. I leam from the press that the government has loaned $700,000 to Newfoundland ; that is a large amount of money. I learn, further, from the press, Mr. Speaker, that on two previous occasions the Canadian government saved Newfoundland from bankruptcy.

speechtext:
It is only proper that the government, before thinking of making another cut in salaries, should ask Great Britain to restore the money which has been advanced to the Newfoundland government. I ask my good friend, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes):	Where did he get that
money? He should get back that money. If it was loaned on the advice of the Prime Minister the Prime Minister was wrong, I am sure if my good friend the Minister of Finance had been left to his own judgment he would never have done it. There are perhaps millions of dollars that should come back from there into the Canadian exchequer to fill the hole that should not be filled by cutting the salaries of the civil servants.
Besides that, I saw in the papers some time ago that a gentleman by the name of Kenneth G. Rea, had sailed on the Empress of Britain to begin the construction of a Canadian legation in Tokio. Is that work undertaken for the relief of unemployment in Canada? Will Canadian materials be used? Will Canadian workmen be employed? Before such work is begun, or before any payment is made on account of it, would it not be better to obtain the assurance that a Japanese legation will be built in Ottawa at the same time?
There is something else, something extraordinary. It is this, that the government has seen fit to make a loan of SI,500,000 to the Canadian Pacific Railway without interest, and at the same time the Canadian Pacific Railway has enough money to buy $2,000,000 worth of dominion bonds bearing interest at four per cent, which means that the government is paying four per cent on 81,500,000 of Canadian money, something very extraordinary-inconceivable. If the government

Salary Deduction Act
forced the Canadian Pacific Railway to pay four per cent on that $1,500,000 it would mean $60,000; in other words that 600 poor little civil servants who will have to suffer a cut of $100 would be exempt, and that the company would have to act in accordance with what is done in business circles, namely that people who have money can pay interest when money is loaned to them.
Another suggestion that I would make, not to the Minister of Finance but to his leader, would be to stop the gambling in wheat. When the matter came before the house the Prime Minister said it would serve no good purpose to give us full details although not only each member as representing the constituency that sent him here was interested but Canada at large. I asked him to clear the galleries in order to take the house into his confidence, but got no answer from him. It is time for him to stop that extravagance, which serves no good purpose but is rather an embarrassment.
There is another thing. When Adam was in the Garden of Eden-

No, there is no question
about women. Some day there may be a lady in the cabinet, but to-day as there are only men, I will speak about the first man. After he ate the apple he was ashamed-

speechtext:
No, it was not an onion,
because at that time there was no culture of onions. Onions grew wild in Egypt then. After he had eaten the forbidden fruit he clothed himself in a fig leaf, but the Prime Minister, the apostle of "Canada first," is riding in an American car, and instead of a fig leaf we find him using a silver maple leaf to hide the American origin of his car. Now here is a most important point. The members of the government get $2,000 a year for 'their cars. I see a car here every day at the door of the east block bearing the number BB-1 or something like that, I have no objection to the number, but I have an objection to Canada's coat of arms being on this car. If the car belongs to the country I do not see why the country has bought for the Prime Minister, the apostle of "Canada first," an American made car. If it is privately owned by that gentleman, he has no right to put the coat of arms of Canada on his car.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONTINUATION OF DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT FROM INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: How do you know?

subtopic: PROPOSED CONTINUATION OF DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT FROM INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Everyone knows, if they
don't they are ignorant. That is the point
I make; first I do not subscribe to paying $400 of my salary to keep that American automobile for the Canadian Prime Minister. Perhaps he does not know, perhaps that car was sold to him under the pretence that it was Canadian made. But if you look at the list of Canadian automobile manufacturers, I defy any hon. member from the other side of the house to say that the Stearns-Knight Company has a factory in Canada. Where is it? No one answers. I say there is none. Well, that is strange. Charity begins at home; why not buy a Canadian made car? Canadian made cars were good enough for Mr. Baldwin, they were good enough for members of the delegations from other parts of the empire who came here last July. But the Prime Minister of Canada has an American car. Canada first!

subtopic: PROPOSED CONTINUATION OF DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT FROM INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONTINUATION OF DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT FROM INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
But there is something
else. If my hon. friend will not keep silence I will tell him some very unpleasant things.
Mr. Chairman, I am a poor man. Most of us are poor men. The indemnity is not a salary. We come here at great sacrifice. During the time I have been here I have heard members from the province of Quebec as well as members of the Progressive party asking for some concession in this matter. Certainly there is not a single member of moderate means who does not attend the sessions of parliament at great sacrifice to his business or his practice, whatever may be his trade or profession. We are here to fulfil a duty. Some people do not agree with the views I express, but I can say that when members are polite to me I am equally polite to them and I treat them just as well as they treat me-some times much better. I must repeat that we come here at a great sacrifice, many members of parliament, gentlemen of culture who have done well in their profession and who have done well for the community, men from every part of the country, from British Columbia to Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. These gentlemen realize that there is such a thing as public spirit in this country and we do not come here merely for the honour of it, which means very little. Indeed, it is troublesome rather than honourable to be a member of parliament, although everyone appreciates the fact that the members of this house have enjoyed the confidence of those who have sent them here. Still, I say, the government must realize that an indemnity of $4,000 does not go very far.
We have to give more to charity to-day than anyone else. It is all very well to quote
Salary Deduction Act

scripture and to say that a cup of cold water given in the Lord's name will not be forgotten, and so on. We have to be charitable not onlly as members of parliament but as private citizens. The fact remains, however, that members of parliament are called upon to make greater sacrifices than the ordinary citizen has to make. The Prime Minister himself has appealed on several occasions to private charity on behalf of the unemployed; he has asked the .'Canadian people to come to the assistance of those who are out of work. The government itself cannot do anything. I do not say that any member of the cabinet is insincere; I believe they are all sincere. But I am sure they realize by now that they are unable to do anything practical for the relief of unemployment.
People speak of the back to the land policy, but that means nothing; it only means that some people are of the opinion that those who are on the land are much better off than the unfortunate people in the city. A good many people who have been in the cities for a considerable length of time are returning now to the paternal shelter because there is no more work for them in the urban centres. Others have therefore to come to their assistance. We find that not only the children, but also the sons in law, the daughters in law and the grandchildren in many cases are coming once more under the paternal roof. According to the last report of the director of unemployment relief, we find that the government gave only three meals on one day to each of the unemployed; they fed these people only one day, and during the other three hundred and sixty-four days these unfortunates had to be fed by private charity. Similarly the government afforded one half of them shelter one night and for the rest of the time private charity was responsible for their accommodation.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONTINUATION OF DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT FROM INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONTINUATION OF DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT FROM INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Oh no; I am going to say all I have to say; I am going to say it for the benefit of those who, having ears to hear and eyes to see, will neither see nor understand.
I am a poor man, Mr. Chairman; my friend from Hochelaga (Mr. St-Pere), is a poor man; so are my friends from St. Henri (Mr. Mercier), from Laurier-Outremont (Mr. Mercier), and from Gaspe (Mr. Brasset), and the majority of us. Now each of us has to subscribe $400 from our indemnity for purposes of private charity, and we have to subscribe that money to some millionaire in the cabinet. The five of us-taking us as examples -have to subscribe $400 each as a contribution either to the Prime Minister, to the Minister 
of Customs or to the hon. gentleman who presides at meetings of the council in the absence of the Prime Minister. I say, we have subscribed that money to millionaires. Is it fair? I do not think anyone will suggest that for a moment. Well, here is the automobile proposal, which the government apparently will not consider. I said last year and I repeat this year that I sincerely believe the salaries paid to members of the cabinet are inadequate. In ordinary times I would be in favour of voting a salary of $25,000 at least to each one of the cabinet ministers and I would be willing to vote a salary of $50,000 to the Prime Minister, because I do believe that the Prime Minister has a more arduous task than the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway or the president of any private concern. At the present time however we are not asking for anything more than what is due to us.
What is improper and indecent is this. The year before the salaries were cut the Prime Minister had sent the then Minister of Labour, Senator Robertson, to the west to get in touch with the people, and that hon. gentleman saw for himself the difficult conditions that existed out there; and after he had been converted he said in answer to my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown) who was pointing out that the farmers of the west had no money. "Why have they not any money?" Senator Robertson went to the west and when he oame back his report was so unfavourable that the Prime Minister could not help realizing the situation and he wanted to do something to assist these people who were in distress. After that it was decided to cut the salaries of the civil service, to cut the salaries of members of the House of Commons and of the Senate and of everyone else, thus increasing the distress that existed in every home.
People everywhere simply could not believe that a member of parliament was subscribing $400 a year to a millionaire like the Prime Minister or a millionaire like the hon. member who replaces that gentleman when he goes away, or a millionaire like the Minister of National Revenue, or for that matter any one of the millionaires in the cabinet. They cannot understand it. They do not realize that so many of us have to subscribe so much each for this purpose. The Prime Minister subscribed to the charity drive in Ottawa $250 of the $400 he is taking from my indemnity.
No one oan justify the discrimination of the cut in the eyes of the people. Only two members besides myself had the courage to speak of this matter in the House of Com-

Salary Deduction Act
mons-my hon. friend from Reauhamois (Mr. Raymond) and my hon. friend from Labelie (Mr. Rourassa). I fancy that there must be remorse among the members of the cabinet.
Do hon members realize that S2.000 is too much to pay for automobile service in these times? You can hire a taxi for a quarter and if you add ten cents to that by way of tip, that makes thirty-five cents; use the taxi four times a day, and does that amount to S2,000? We have simply got to practise economy, and ministers of the government would do well if they would give back to the state the amount that they have received in respect of automobiles during the past two years.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONTINUATION OF DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT FROM INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Then I will continue. I can imagine a meeting of the council. At that meeting will be certain ministers who are in touch with the people, while there are others who are not; there will be those who know of the hardships, the poverty and the misery which exists in so many homes, and there will be others who are quite satisfied so long as they themselves are not hungry or thirsty. A discussion arises as to a cut in salaries and I can see someone saying, "Ontario has given us a lead, we must follow." Probably other ministers stated their objections, but the thing was done.
I appreciate the fact that hon. members on both sides of the house are so courteous in listening to what I say. They are all supporting the stand wdiich some of us took last year and the year before. It is to be hoped that there will be no cut this year in the salaries of the civil servants or anyone receiving moneys from the exchequer. So much the better.
I know that hon. members of this house are not hard hearted; they are compassionate and they suffer from the bottom of their hearts when they see a man who has not enough to eat, who cannot clothe his children in order to send them to school to receive an education. If we had 84,000 per year, if the ministers were allowed only 8400 in lieu of private motor cars, conditions would be different because we could do much with that extra $400 to relieve those in distress. That is what should be done.
Private charity has done a lot in this regard. The Prime Minister has made an appeal to private charity, but he then goes ahead and cuts it by ten per cent. Many people have charitable obligations. I met a man who works here in the building, receiving a salary of 880 or $90 per month. He told me that his priest had said that he should support the unemployed, that the civil service had been asking him to subscribe to the Ottawa drive, and yet he was supporting two of his children with their families. I told that man he was already doing enough, that it was not necessary for him to subscribe to church charities or to the Ottawa drive. I told him that if he continued to do what he had been doing he could be cited as an example to anyone. Private charities are doing considerable to relieve conditions; the work of the St. Vincent de Paul society, the Salvation Army and the Red Cross has been marvellous.

I have listened in patience -to my hon. friend for forty minutes and I think I have a right not to be interrupted while I occupy the time of the house for such few moments as may be necessary while I reply to the statements which he has made, following which I shall submit to any questions which my hon. friend may wish to put to me.
My hon. friend has said that Newfoundland means no more to Canada than does some foreign country. I do not think he will have many other members in the house or people in the country who will subscribe to that kind of view. Newfoundland is the oldest dominion under the crown. It has been, and quite properly so, one of the boasts of the British people that they have always met .their obligations. There has never been a

default. When it was open to us in cooperation with the mother country, to lend a hand to the oldest dominion, a sister dominion,
I claim we are entitled to consideration for having come to her assistance under those circumstances. What we did was to say to the banks who came to the assistance of Newfoundland at that time, that we would stand behind them in cooperation with the mother country in case eventually Newfoundland found it impossible to meet her just obligations. So far from being criticized, I think we have every reason to take credit for having lent that helping hand under those circumstances. I do not need to place it on the ground of patriotic consideration. If, as has been the case in times past, we 'have come to the assistance of those who have met with disaster in foreign countries, surely we are entitled to come to the assistance of our sister dominion, Newfoundland, in the circumstances.
My hon. friend has referred to the fact that we have sent money to Tokyo to build a legation. We have done nothing of the bind. We have not sent a dollar. That arrangement in detail will, I have no doubt, be discussed when the estimates of the Department of External Affairs are under review. When it is discussed, I have every reason to believe the arrangement which was entered into because of the patriotic action of the Minister to Japan will be approved by this house and by the country. It is fortunate that we have in the public service of Canada a man with such high ideals of the public service as has the Minister to Japan.
My hon. friend used an argument which I know rolls like a sweet morsel upon the tongues of some hon. gentlemen, especially when they are discussing before a popular audience the shortcomings of the administration, when he referred to the faet that the government had lent $1,500,000 to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. That is one way of putting the situation. As a matter of fact, whether the advance was right or not, what we did was not to give the money to the Canadian Pacific Railway because it was the Canadian Pacific Railway. We had decided that inasmuch as the shops of that railway would not be opened and there would be poverty and want on the part of those who had hitherto been employed, rather than have those people go upon relief, it would be not only humane but fitting to provide a sum of money which would enable the shops to be opened, thereby affording employment to those people. All that will come as an ultimate loss to the treasury is the interest upon that sum between the time it was advanced and the time when it is repaid as I

believe it will be by the Canadian Pacific. If the payment is not made for a period of years, tihe cost to the exchequer will not be greater or will be very little more than would have been the case if money had had to be handed out by way of relief.
My hon. friend has said by way of criticism -and I have heard this argument before-at the same time as this government gave SI,- 500,000 to the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian Pacific bought $2,000,000 worth of bonds upon which the dominion is paying interest at 44 per cent. That statement is absolutely untrue. In the first place the Canadian Pacific Railway did not buy one dollar's worth of bonds. That is the fact to start with, but even if we asume it had done so, there would be nothing inconsistent in the two positions because the Canadian Pacific Railway is the custodian of trust funds, pension funds, sinking funds, which have to be invested, and it would be quite fitting and proper under those circumstances for the Canadian Pacific Railway to make truslt funds and invest them in trustee securities which would be the securities of the Dominion of Canada. Therefore there is nothing inconsistent in that position.
My hon. friend harps upon a familiar chord, which I have not any doubt affords sweet music in the ears of those who want to indulge in the old political pastime of spellbinding, when he deals with the question of $2,000 to ministers in lieu of motor cars. In the first place this has not been $2,000 for the last two years. It has been $1,800, because it has been subject to a deduction of ten per cent. Let me say to my hon. friend that under previous administrations these sums of money did not more than pay for the gasoline, repairs and extra tires of cars of ministers. It barely would pay for the salaries of the chauffeurs, every one of whom was provided by the government and not one of whom, if my memory serves me rightly, received less than $1,440 a year. It did not take account of depreciation of cars, some of which cost as much as $5,000 and $6,000, and most of which were imported cars at that, I may tell my hon. friend. The reason the cars were taken away from ministers and an allowance given in lieu of them was to save the public treasury some tens of thousands of dollars. I have not the figures before me, but I have perused them in times past and I may say to my hon. friend that this allowance to ministers to-day in lieu of motor cars means that that service costs the public treasury not much if any more than one-third the cost under the old arrangement sanctioned by previous administrations. I am not going to defend the amount of emoluments ministers may receive. I have
had some experience in public life, and I may say to my hon. friend that any minister who is devoted to his duties leaves the service of his country poorer than when he entered it. When I say that I include as well the allowance for motor cars. It might be good politics for the ministers to say, "No allowance, we will walk." But I say that would cost this country more than the allowance of $1,800, because ten or fifteen minutes in the time of a minister on a busy day is of the utmost importance to the country, if the country's business is to be run expeditiously.
I submit my hon. friend went a little too far when he brought the name of the Prime Minister into the discussion in connection with a matter which, after all, is his personal and private affair. I say to my hon. friend that the car owned by the Prime Minister was purchased by him in Canada as a second hand car, from a man in needy circumstances who wanted money. And when my hon. friend suggests that his only contribution to charity was $250-

I have been wondering what they will think of the hon. member for Temis-couata when, from his remarks, they must readily realize that he begrudges making his contribution along with the contributions which must be made through the sacrifice of all the people of Canada, if we are to get over the period through which we are passing to-day.
I know about the demands made upon members of parliament. If my memory serves me correctly, I recall that when I first entered this house the indemnity was only $1,500 a year. I may say I found it hard scratching in the earlier days to make ends meet,-not that I did so, certainly, from my indemnity. Notwithstanding the demands made upon members of parliament the fact is that having regard to the costs of living, leaving aside any other considerations, a member of parliament is as well paid to-day at $3,600 as he was three years ago at $4,000. But apart from that-and I do not place my discussion upon a money basis at all-when in our need we must ask sacrifices on the part, of our people to help us through this period of depression, a condition which we share in common with the whole world, we could not hold up our heads as members of this House of Commons if we asked everybody in Canada to make sacrifices but refused to make them ourselves. Let me say to the hon. member for Temis-couata that I know something of conditions in Ottawa. I know of no city in Canada where there is less distress and want than is to be found in this very city. I shall go a little farther and say that I have great admiration for the civil servants of Canada. I have seen much of them, and I know that no more loyal service could be given by any individual than is given by many civil servants to this dominion. Many of them who are serving the crown to-day are doing so at a sacrifice, because to my certain knowledge some of them are in receipt of salaries much smaller than they could receive from private employers. But the type of patriotism found in the civil service goes all down the line. I say to hon. members opposite that the great majority of the civil servants of Ottawa realize the necessity for this sacrifice, and are prepared to make their contribution. I say particularly to the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier), that there was a feeling of

delight on the part of civil servants when they learned that we proposed to ask for a contribution of only ten per cent this year; many of them expected it would be much higher. We are not seeking any undue sacrifice by asking the civil servants to make a ten per cent contribution. I know of no country where it is not being done. In Australia, instead of ten per cent they are taking from 15 per cent to 20 per cent. In the great republic to the south of us, with all their wealth, last year they called upon the civil servants to take a month's holidays without pay. There is a further proposal which may or may not go through, that there should be a cut of 11 per cent on top of that.
Mr. Chairman, I do not purpose further to labour this discussion. I do not wish to be accused of lecturing; I do not wish the hon. member for Temiscouata to think that I am censorious of his rights in this committee. I do submit however that at a time like the present if we cannot forget party we ought at least realize that there are serious problems confronting this country, and that we would be better employed in devoting ourselves to the consideration of the matter in hand rather than indulging in political spell-binding such as we used to indulge in on the hustings on the back concessions in the piping times of prosperity.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the Minister of Finance has said, we have had in the last few minutes two political speeches intended for consumption on the hustings. Onet he said, was delivered by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), and I suggest one was delivered by himself. Perhaps I may be allowed to go back to the resolution before us, which appears as follows:
That it is expedient to continue in force the provisions of the Salary Deduction Act 1932, until the 31st day of March, 1934, and to provide that the provisions of the said act shall apply to the indemnities of members of the Senate and House of Commons for the session of parliament which commenced on the 6th day of October, 1932.
As the minister tried to argue, it may be necessary that there should be a continuation of the legislation of last year. But I should like to ask him why in this resolution he deliberately singles out members of the House of Commons and the Senate. Why does he find it necessary to add the words:
That the provisions of the said act shall apply to the indemnities of members of the Senate and House of Commons for the session, of parliament which commenced on the 6th day of October, 1932.
Are they an entirely different class of people? Why are we singled out? Why did the min-

Salary Deduction Act
ister say a few moments ago that we should be glad to give $400 from our indemnities? Sure, we are glad to give more. How much did my hon. friend give to charity last year? I have no doubt he gave three times $400. Then why should the Minister of Finance come and say we should give this $400 towards charity or poor relief? I say our salaries as members of parliament have nothing to do with our subscriptions to charity.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am afraid this resolution was hurriedly drawn, the Minister of Finance yesterday had to rise in this house and ask the indulgence of the house because he did not put his resolution on the order paper.	Of	course	we	decided unanimouslyto let	the	matter	go	through without the
regular notice. But let us see what actually is going to continue under this resolution. In 1932 this house and Senate passed chapter 52, an act to provide for a deduction from compensation in the public service. In clause 2, subsection (b), it says:
"Member of the public service of Canada" means every officer,	clerk and employee in any
branch	or	portion	of	the public service of
Canada, to whom any compensation is paid, either directly or indirectly, out of the revenue of His Majesty in respect of his government of Canada, other than the Governor General of Canada, the lieutenant-governors of the several provinces of Canada, the members of the judicial'}', and the members of the military, naval and air forces of Canada, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police,-
Now, Mr. Chairman, the exemptions start from the Governor General and go down to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. These exemptions are going to be asked again under this resolution which we are now considering. I wish emphatically to protest, as a member of this parliament and as a citizen of Canada. If there is going to be a reduction, whether 10 or 20 or 50 per cent, in my indemnity as a member of the House of Commons, or if there is going to be a reduction in the salaries of light-keepers, there should be a reduction all round. For instance, my hon. friend must have noticed a few days ago that in his constituency a poor light-keeper, a returned soldier, was fired from his position on Green island and a new man appointed, not a returned soldier, and this new man has to take a reduction of ten per cent, while the Governor General and the lieutenant-governors and the military and naval forces and the judges are going to get their whole salary. I say that is not right. It may be all right for the Minister of Justice to see that the judges get 100 per cent while the light-keeper on Green island get3 only 90 per cent, but
the people of this country believe in fair treatment for every one, and I for one protest against this resolution, and before I conclude I am going to ask that the committee rise to enable the finance minister to redraft the resolution so that every one gets the same cut as the light-keeper and the poor charwomen and the elevator men and the $100 postmasters and everybody else.
Now let us consider this matter. The finance minister said that the civ:l servants were delighted to accept this ten per cent cut. Well, the Minister of Finance may move in different company from what I do. I have never met one oivil servant who accepted this cut with good grace. Why? If we are going to fix the salaries of civil servants every year as conditions may warrant, give them $1,000 this year and $1,200 next and $2,000 when the Grits get back in power and we have prosperous times, and then when the Tories get back in the next fifty years cut them down to $500, then I say, it is all right to make this deduction this year. But it must not be forgotten that the civil servants, whether times are good or bad, whether the cost of living is high or low, get only the same salary. Consequently I say it is not fair to these civil servants, who have made plans and commitments thinking they were going to get a certain sum, to have to take a cut of ten per cent. I know that if my hon. friend goes on the hustings at the next election and tries to defend the policies of this government by saying it was the right thing to do to cut these civil servants, who in any case we could perhaps do without, there will be certain people who will applaud. It will be fairly good stuff on the public platform. But after all is said and done the people of this country are sane. A great many shibboleths have been discussed on the public platform, but I have confidence in the sanity of the people of Canada, and in spite of the quack remedies that are offered them I say they are sane and sensible and are going to agree that if they require a postmaster he is worth $100 if he is worth anything; if they require a customs officer he is worth the amount which was agreed to be paid him under the Civil Service Act. And, coming back to the matter of salaries of members of parliament, last year I went back to my constituency and the province of Nova Scotia and I have yet to hear one criticism because I stood up in this parliament and said I was worth $4,000 and had a contract with the people of Canada to pay me that amount. I say to every hon. member of this house or the Senate that he is worth the money which the people of this country contracted to pay him. This is not a salary,
Salary Deduction Act

it is only an indemnity, and every hon. member knows that we do not get enough to half meet our expenses, we leave our businesses and give our time and any ability we possess and do our duty as far as in us lies for the people of the country. No right thinking man in this country grudges the member of parliament $4,000, because he knows that instead of having $4,000 at the end of the year he has nothing or less than nothing.
Now, Mr. Chairman, what is the idea of these exemptions? Why are we asked to pass this act? Have we again to fight the battle we fought last year, when members of the militja and the navy, the judiciary and the lieutenant-governors were to get their full salaries, while the page boys and the charwomen were to take a ten per cent cut from their widow's mite that the people of the country are paying them. What have we seen in the last twenty-four hours? Look what these poor charwomen met this morning. My hon. friend the finance minister talks about economy; he says expenses have to be cut. Think of these poor charwomen coming here at six o'clock in the morning, picking up the newspaper and reading that they are going to lose ten per cent of the pay the government gives them, and on the other page that the government has appointed Milton N. Campbell at a salary of $10,000 to the tariff board. Is that the kind of economy my hon. friend professes, taking from the charwomen and the elevator men and giving Milton N. Campbell $10,000-

If my hon. friend wants to economize I will be glad to help him, I will show him where it is not necessary to take ten per cent from the charwomen and the elevatormen and the lighthouse keepers. Someone mentioned Tokyo this afternoon. The gentleman who is the ambassador or commissioner or whatever he is, Mr. Marler, is a personal friend of mine, but since this government in their wisdom have settled the question that Japanese oranges are not oranges but tangerines there is no further necessity to have Mr. Marler in Japan. This government raised the tariff in 1931, putting a duty on oranges from foreign countries. The Japanese government at once protested, and taking a leaf out of the Prime Minister's book they said, "If you put an embargo on coal from Russia we will put an embargo on goods coming from Canada to Japan." They were asked by Mr. Marler why they took this attitude and he was told that rMr. Duff.]
it was because this government put a high duty on Japanese oranges. The result was that there was consternation in Japan and Canada. Well, the governor in council solemnly gathered his ministers around him and after some length of time, consulting Webster's dictionary they saw that tangerines were oranges; it said, "Tangerine-see oranges." Then they looked up oranges and they found that one variety of oranges was known as tangerines and another as margarines. And this government, which is so busy that a minister cannot waste fifteen minutes to walk from one department to another, passed an order in council declaring that oranges from Japan were not oranges at all but tangerines.
Now why not let us economize? Here we are going to be asked to vote $70,900 for the Tokyo legation. In the first place, Mr. Chairman, as you know, in the last two or three years our trade has fallen off more than fifty per cent and I say that if the government would take this amount which they intend to spend in Tokyo-not for business, because they do not want business from Japan-and would use it for the purpose I am going to suggest, they would be able to avoid this ten per cent cut in the salaries of lighthouse keepers and others in Canada, including the salary of the man on Green island in the county of Richmond, Nova Scotia. They have also cut the salary of the lighthouse keeper on Cranberry island. Perhaps the Minister of Finance read the Halifax papers a day or two ago; if so he will have noticed that in the terriffic storm that occurred on the Atlantic coast last week the situation was so grave that the lighthouse keeper and his family at that point could not get outside the light for thirty-six hours. The breakwater as well as the oribwork surrounding the island was washed away; the light was shaking back and forth and it was expected to be hurled into the sea. Yet my hon. friend and the government solemnly propose a vote of $70,900 towards the Japanese legation, while they are taking ten peir cent off the salary of the lighthouse keeper and his poor wife on Cranberry island. Is that fair? Is it decent? If they want to save the country, if my hon. friends opposite want to save the government, surely they can do better than taking ten per cent from the lighthouse keepers and the page boys, the elevator men and the ordinary postmasters throughout this country. If they cannot do better than that then I suggest with all deference that they should resign and let someone else take charge.

Yes, even to save the government. I do say that if the government want to economize they must cut down expenses that can be done without. Let us take, for instance, the amount which it is proposed to spend in connection with our representation at Washington-$92,900. I am not going to be personal at all. This office was created and opened by the Liberal government, and I am criticizing neither the office nor the individual; but I do say that in this time of stress and strain, when it is necessary for the country to practise economy in every direction, and when the government is taking ten per cent from the $100 received by the postmaster, or $10, and when we are talking about cooperation all the time and even amalgamation, we should pay some attention to a matter of this sort. I say, close the Washington office until we get back to better times and let the British ambassador do our work over there. That would result in a saving of $92,000. The Liberal party established the office and we are proud of it, but we could afford to close it for the present. What my hon. friends opposite are doing is not building up but tearing down; they are even tearing up the page boy's little cheque every fortnight.
There are further items in the estimates to which I might refer; some of them we could veiy well do without. For instance, here is an item of $38,500 to provide for the payment of salaries and expenses in connection with St. Lawrence ship canal surveys investigation. It seems to me that, especially after Mr. Roosevelt's election as president of the United States, there is no hope in the near future of this canal being built by Canada or the United States, and consequently there is no need of surveys. Let us wait until the country is in a position to build a canal or to make some arrangement regarding it. At any rate, there is an amount which would make up the ten per cent on certain salaries which the minister thinks he is obliged to reduce. And I might go on to deal with other items.
While I am willing if necessary, and if it is in the interests of the country, to have salaries reduced, I do think that it is poor policy, it is bad business to economize in the way this government is doing, because it is
Salary Deduction Act

simply withdrawing from circulation in the country millions of dollars. Financiers who know more about money matters than I do have told me that one dollar goes around seventeen times; so that if you multiply the amount which the Minister of Finance thinks he will save by means of this resolution and the act which he proposes to introduce, you can readily see that if that money were put to work in Canada there would not be as much unemployment as there is at the present time. This is following a penny wise and pound foolish policy, because every person who has had to take this reduction has had to reduce his budget. Expenditures have been reduced and for every dollar Which a civil servant does not spend, hundreds of other people suffer. As I said a moment ago, there is a class which is being exempted, and this should not be. We are being solemnly asked to adopt this resolution, we will be asked to pass a bill similar to the one passed last year under which lighthouse keepers, postmasters and other civil servants will be cut ten per cent, but I think the minister should amend his resolution and strike out the reference to members of the House of Commons and members of the Senate. In the act passed last year and in the present resolution it is stated definitely that members of the House of Commons and members of the Senate have to take this ten per cent reduction. Why trot them out to the public gaze, why not leave the poor devils alone? It is bad enough that they should lose $400 without deliberately singling them out for mention. No mention is made of the high hats in the militia, no mention is made of the cocked hats in the navy, but the poor members of parliament are trotted out for mention. Subsection (b) of section 2 of the act states:
-and includes members of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, and members, officers, clerks and employees of every commission, board or corporate body.
The minister should move that this committee rise and report progress in order that he may have an opportunity to redraft his resolution. He could come back with a new bill based upon his new resolution, and we could then consider the matter. If the lighthouse keepers, the postmasters and other civil servants are to take a ten per cent reduction-a twenty per cent reduction if necessary-the judges, the lieutenant-governors, the members of the militia and the navy and everybody else should take the same reduction.

There are too many cabinet ministers; there is too much duplication between provincial and federal services. For instance, we have provincial departments of labour and a federal Department of Labour. I am suggesting if the government is prepared to cut down expenditures I am prepared to support it, and that is going a long way for a Liberal. Mr. Chairman, last year I opposed this legislation, and must maintain the same position this year. I can sympathize with the desire of the Minister of Finance to balance his budget, but it seems to me there are other ways in which this can be done than by cutting down the salaries of the civil servants. There is undoubtedly a good deal in what the member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn) has just said, that there are a great many places where economies

might be effected. I think undoubtedly the government of Canada costs more than it should, but I do not believe that the economy should be effected by cutting down the salaries especially of the poorer paid civil servants. The largest item that we have in our expenditures is that recognized generally as uncontrollable expenditure, most of it interest on bonded debt. It seems to me that the finance minister might very well consider the possibility of cutting down that item. During this time of depression almost everyone has taken his loss except those who hold bonds. The finance minister said a little while ago that he thought possibly a member of parliament receiving $3,600 now is as well off as he was a few years ago when he received $4,000. I think that is probably true. But if it is true it means that the man who has a bond for $4,000 should be receiving only $3,600. I think that is drawing it very mild indeed. On the minister's own argument, that money has increased in purchasing power, he must recognize that bondholders to-day are drawing a larger amount than that to which they are justly entitled, regard being paid to the altered buying power of the dollar. It would seem to me that the government ought to take into consideration some form of conversion by which the present bonded indebtedness would be reduced so that it could be handled. I suppose the easiest and simplest way to do that would be by a form of inflation. It might possibly be done, of course, by a cutting down of the interest charges in one way or another. It seems to me we cannot maintain the policy of paying interest on our enormous debts, and especially trying to do it by means of reductions in salaries.
Again let me point out that legislation of this kind savours of class legislation, because it bears directly upon one class of citizens, namely, the civil servants, and others who draw their salaries from the government. Why should not the extra amount be raised by a steeply graduated tax on all incomes, not selecting the civil servants, but putting a tax-an extra tax-on all salaries?
I would point out that this so-called "economy" of this kind is no way of solving the economic problem that confronts Canada at the present time. I think it is recognized by all economists that what we need to-day is increased purchasing power, but legislation of this kind leads to decreased purchasing power. When the ten per cent cut was first made I think the merchants of Ottawa received a very salutary lesson in economics, because most of them experienced in their decreased sales the effect of the cut. The great majority 
of people spend what is coming to them, so if they have ten per cent less to buy with, that means ten per cent less business. I cannot see that for the sake of saving a few dollars we are justified in adding to the general depression.

Mr. Chairman, my taking part in this debate at this moment is inspired by the views just expressed by the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn). I would not like the country to believe that there is ,a lack of sentiment in this house in favour of the principle underlying this resolution. I know that many Liberals, both in and out of the house, favour economy, and it is but fair, not only to the country generally but to the party I represent, that we be given an opportunity to express our side of the case.
I do not think it is a good argument against this resolution to point out that the government should have practised economy in other fields. If that is any argument at all, it is one in favour of the resolution. I do agree with my ihon. friends on this side that further economies might be practised in connection with other items in the estimates, but the proper time to point that out is when these estimates are before us. If we want further economy in the general expenditures of the government, we should be ready ourselves to give an example. We should accept this deduction with grace and dignity. I believe in this contribution-1 prefer calling it a contribution rather than a deduction-first, because of the material advantages it will give to the government in the expedition of business, and, second, because of the moral example given to the country in that, realizing

Salary Deduction Act
the serious plight of the country, realizing the position in which thousands of men, women and children are placed in this period of crisis and depression, we are willing not merely to talk about it, to multiply words and speeches about it, but to contribute some of our own indemnities to help the government solve this great problem.
It has been said that the indemnity is in the nature of a fixed obligation on the part of the government. I do not agree with that statement, because the amount of the indemnity has been changed from time to time. Some years ago it was increased; times were prosperous and it was thought that members might be given a little more for their work and the expenses of their stay in Ottawa. The same principle should work the other way: when times are hard, when money is scarce and everybody is making sacrifices, members of parliament should be willing to agree to a reduction in their indemnities.
All public bodies are making similar deductions. We will have to do it in Montreal, if I may be permitted to cite that as an example. When I first took part in the administration of the city of Montreal, my colleagues and myself were hoping that we might be able to carry on without reducing salaries. But we found that that would be impossible. There was not only the financial burden of the salaries, but there was also the pressure from public opinion which demanded that the municipal employees should do their share. We have 40,000 unemployed heads of families in Montreal, which means a very large population of unemployed. I hope I will be understood when I say that I think anyone who to-day has a position and is in receipt of a salary is in a preferred position, especially when compared to those heads of families who although willing to work are unable to find anything to do. This applies not only to the higher salaried people, but even to the charwomen who were mentioned a moment ago. With all due respect to this class of people, I think that even a charwoman who to-day is employed and is receiving a salary is in a preferred position when compared to the many mothers of families who are willing to work but who are unable to find employment. I do not think it is unreasonable to ask these people to contribute their small part to the general welfare of the country.
Another argument advanced is that members of the house, being public men, are asked to contribute heavily to private charity. We all know that these demands have grown with the increased difficulties of the times, but the committee must realize that in times
of stress like these we cannot rely on private charity alone. Private charity is absolutely unable to meet the demands made upon it, and must be assisted by the immense contributions of the federal, the provincial and municipal governments. I say without hesitation that I would rather see every hon. member of this house reduce his contributions to private charity by S400 and contribute that amount to be used in a public way for the dispensation of relief. It would be absolutely impossible for a city like Montreal to rely upon private donations alone. I would rather see this extra amount expended through the federal government and used in a public way in order to meet the extraordinary demands of the day.
I am in favour of this resolution. I do not oare what its phraseology may be so long as it says what it means. I am quite sure that when the government asks parliament, through its members, to contribute to the general need of the day it will receive a happy reply, not only from the government side but from all sides of the house. I do not think this question should be approached either with levity or with the idea of taking a bitter stand against the resolution; it should not be contended that simply because our indemnities are being reduced by ten per cent the whole fabric of the country is going to fall to pieces. On the contrary, I say in all modesty that we should accept this reduction with grace and dignity. That is my stand upon the matter.

If I cannot say that, I would suggest to the Minister of Finance or to the hon. member for Long Lake (Mr. Cowan) that they have legislation enacted in order to make the person of the Prime Minister sacred in accordance with Roman law, or have it enacted that he is a god and that it is a sin to contradict him or to mention his name in a debate. I have never been personal to any member in the house. The only thing I have done has been to defend my rights as a member.
While I mentioned many matters in connection with the senators, the Minister of Finance said nothing in answer to my suggestion. I hope be will accept it, because it was made in all earnestness.
As regards the Canadian Pacific, we have seen in the press that the government has lent money without interest to that railway company. The Minister of Finance says that this has been done in order to give an opportunity to the Canadian Pacific to open the Angus shops. Well, this was a hold-up of the government on the part of the Canadian Pacific. They had the money to employ the men, but they wanted it without interest. As to their subscription afterwards to the dominion loan, what I have said is exactly what has been reported in the press.
As regards Newfoundland, a matter of sentiment, which I understand, arises; people may have friends or relatives there. That is all very well. The hon. member for Long Lake will understand my point as well as anyone. What I say is that this country of ours extends from the Atlantic to the Pacific, including Prince Edward Island. I am more interested in Canada than in Newfoundland, and Newfoundland being outside the boundaries of Canada is no more to me than is the United States or any other country which is outside -the boundaries of this dorninian. The people in my county will be ready to do anything for those in any other province within those limits, but we are interested in Newfoundland only inasmuch as our people here are all free from care. We have first to look 
after our own people in Long Lake or in St. Peters or Temiscoua-ta, wherever they are in C-ainada. As long as there is in this country one man who is not looked -after, we cannot do anything outside. That is my view abou-t the matter. I may be wrong; I may be right. I respect the opinion -of others on that point-. The question is not one of sentiment; it is one of helping first the Canadian who lives in this country or anyone who has been living here for years. It is the same Canada first policy.
As regards the legation at Tokyo, there is no smoke without fire. I do not know what happened, but what I said was after having read a dispatch in the press about the trip of a Montreal architect to Tokyo in connection with the matter. Mr. Marler might be the most wonderful minister since Metternich and Talleyrand, and he must be very popular with His Imperial Highness and the royal family, and so forth. The Japanese people are good people; they are very well represented in Canada, but my point is that it is absurd to start a Canadian building in Japan until she builds a legation building in Canada and gives the same chance to Canadian workmen in Canada as Canada gives to Japanese workmen there.
In the -morning papers I have seen something in the way of educational pictures, "-the spice of the program," something from the ginger group. There was the picture of Mr. Milton Campbell, the newly appointed tariff commissioner. I was glad to learn this afternoon that he -has been highly recommended by the KIu Klux Kl-an. It is fair that he has been appointed in lieu of Conservative members who could do better. Mr. Milton Campbell has w'on the race over his illustrious namesake, Sir Malcolm Campbell, the speed king, and made a new record. I wonder if his accomplishments on the tariff board will be just as notable as those of Sir Malcolm Campbell at Daytona Beach. May I suggest to the government that they retain another five per cent from his salary, if the ten per cent is to apply, in order to supply the newly appointed commissioner with an encyclopedia of general knowledge, because the Minister of Finance knows that there is a great love of books in the far corner, and if he looks back at the speeches delivered by the new commissioner while a member of parliament, he will see there are many quotations. If he does not want the new commissioner to build a shrine in the basement of some printing office, he must supply him with books-and what would be better for him than a nice encyclopedia of general knowledge, the speeches delivered during the election and afterwards by the Prime Minister.

In saying a few words in connection with this resolution I shall try to confine myself to the subject matter before us. In the first place I am rigidly opposed to the principle of the resolution itself, and when I say the principle of the resolution I mean the horizontal cut of ten per cent. I am not opposed to a reduction in salaries, a reduction in members' indemnities if such be necessary, but I am absolutely opposed to any reduction in the salaries of those who are getting too little now on which to live. If I gathered his words correctly, the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) stated that even a charwoman getting a very small salary should feel privileged to make a contribution at this time. I believe, however, she would feel more privileged if it were not for the fact that some of the contribution she makes goes into the pockets of people who have more money than they know what to do with.
I should like to draw to the attention of the minister some facts with which I am familiar, and I believe that some of the circumstances I shall outline are typical of the conditions in which many civil servants find themselves. I refer to a man in the city of Vancouver who was a full time employee of the government. Because of lack of work in his department he was put on part time, with the result that he is engaged two and one-half hours a day at forty cents an hour, giving him a daily wage of SI. From that dollar there is a ten per cent reduction. Although he receives only S5.40 a week, yet he is working and is not eligible for relief, although he is a married man with a wife and one child. How can a married man support his wife and family on $5.40 a week? I should much rather see a greater percentage deducted from my indemnity, and from the indemnities of hon. members, in order that the salaries of these men might be left as they are. It is all very well to talk about making our contributions, but when from a wage of $1 per day there is a deduction of ten cents I do not think we would urge that conditions are at all equitable, particularly when we know that others of us are getting enough to live decently on, under present standards of living. I am convinced the Minister of Finance is not unmindful of existing conditions, and I should be very happy if he could see his way clear to bring in an amendment to the present legislation which would relieve from the proposed reduction those receiving salaries under a certain amount. I leave that suggestion with the Minister of Finance and with the government. I suggest the minimum should not be lower than $1,000. The loss to
the country would not be great, and the feeling of goodwill would be worth far more than any inconvenience the loss of revenue might cause. I ask the Minister of Finance to consider my suggestion, and if it meets with the approval of the government I should like to see an amendment to that effect.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief in my remarks. It is admitted by all that we are undergoing a very serious crisis. Our governments request the co-operation of all citizens, rich and poor. It strikes me that this resolution might have been less exacting from those who are in poor circumstances or in receipt of small wages, and demand larger contributions from those who receive large salaries. When our soldiers were fighting for their country on the battlefield, even sacrificing their life, the large financiers remained at home taking advantage of the war to pile up immense wealth. To-day, the crisis we are undergoing calls for the co-operation of all. I am ready to do my share and to accept a cut in my indemnity; on the other hand I think it reasonable and just to exact a larger contribution from those who receive salaries of $3,000, $5,000, $10,000 and $15,000, than from those who are in receipt of $1,500 to $1,800. On behalf of my constituents, my province, and the whole country, I request that the government compel those who have wealth to contribute on a larger scale and collect a smaller contribution from those who receive wages hardly sufficient to give bread to their dependents. We have in this country a large number of millionaires who contribute nothing to the revenues of the State. They have loaned their millions to the government, at 6 per cent; they own no property and pay no taxes; therefore, I deem it only just to request them to contribute their quota in order to help the country to extricate itself from the straits we are in.

Mr. Chairman, when the house rose at six o'clock, I was stating that it is the workmen and labourers who have suffered the most during the war. In the present crisis, it is the same people who suffer the most, and governments have failed to understand their responsibility and duties when, instead of helping this class in weathering the crisis, they have contributed in increasing the number of unemployed by dismissing a considerable number of employees.
In requesting civil servants, members, and senators to contribute in relieving the distress,
I think the government is wrong because in cutting down the salaries of civil servants they simply decrease their purchasing power. We must, in order to remedy the financial crisis take effective means, create this purchasing power which at present is lacking. All our financial and industrial institutions have contributed largely to spread the crisis by diminishing the purchasing power of the people and dismissing a large number of employees.
If there be a class of society which should contribute to relieve the present day distress, it is certainly the one that profited the most and even disregarded the laws of this country by overcapitalizing its enterprises and taking more than reasonable profits. It strikes me that these industrialists and financiers, instead of sitting on their capital, should have placed it at the disposal of the-ir employees so as to afford work or at least help to those who assisted them in amassing this enormous wealth.
Mr. Chairman, it is more than time that this government seriously considered the enactment of social laws to restrain the ambition of financiers. I recall a few years ago an act was passed by this House to prevent trade coalitions. However, daily, we witness certain corporations absorbing other companies and organizing coalitions which greatly contribute to increase the hardships of those who suffer and to maintain the cost of production at a high level. It would be necessary, to-day, that laws be enacted to force these over-capitalized corporations to revert to their original capital so as to out down the cost of production. Is it reasonable, is it rational, that a government which needs revenues should apply to financial companies and offer them a rate of interest as high as and per cent, such as those that were granted by the government, not on the last loan but on previous loans. I think that the
Salary Deduction Act

country is quite solvent and if there is a borrower who should pay the lowest rate, it is certainly the government; a rate of 3J or 4 per cent would have been sufficient. The administration boasts of having done a great deal for the unemployed. The government had blank cheques voted to them so as to help the unemployed and distribute doles-[DOT] an entirely false and immoral principle. Our frienids, sir, on the extreme left have charged the present regime with favouring capitalists. Our governmental regime is not one of capitalism. If to-day, it seems to be so, it is because the members who compose it are inclined to favour financial interests to the detriment of the other classes of society. A free hand was allowed to these financiers thus fostering their inclination and ambition. When in the future we grant powers to certain companies who solicit the government, it should be stipulated that their capital can no further be increased, and that over-capitalization be prohibited in order to forestall coalitions as they exist to-day. We have mergers in lumber, water powers, gasoline, and coal etc. etc. These abuses should cease and we should not allow that the people be thus exploited. Speeches delivered by our friends on the extreme left are purely academic. They are the kind of people who wish to appear in the limelight, besides being extremists. What is needed is not a change but a reform of the present regime. A sound and wise administration must be given to the country in keeping with the interests and needs of the people. What is especially wanted at the moment, is work. It is absolutely impossible for governments, either federal, provincial or municipal to supply work to all. Corporations will be compelled to carry on their operations and it will be necessary for the government to permit them, through a moderate tariff policy, to sell their products with advantage on the world markets. Tariff barriers have had no other result than to paralyze industry and bring hardship upon us. What is needed is not a change in the administrative regime, but a reform; tariffs must be reduced and our products must find a market abroad in order to give work to our people.
We must be on the alert; the storm is on the horizon; we must not rest on laurels won by false and sham promises; we must return to a sound policy, one profitable not only to some but to all. The weak point of the present administration is to ignore such a policy. I think, if the government adopted higher ideals, we could easily weather this crisis by giving work to those who have none, creating this absolutely necessary purchasing power, and this aim will not be reached by

thanking employees for their services, and cutting down their salaries, or allowing higher officials to enjoy large salaries and preventing the lower classes in the public service earning a decent livelihood.
Mr. Chairman, as I stated a short while ago, the time has come not to change our economic regime but to reform it and return to a sound policy, one of patriotism, and not one of sham as advocated in order to capture the popular vote and later on favor friends, increase the number of large financiers and drive the people to greater distress.

Prior to the dinner hour, however, there were two spokesmen from this corner representing, as they would suggest, labour particularly. I do not admit that myself because I also represent labour; in fact my whole constituency is a labouring constituency. The point of view of the direct labour representatives as expressed more particularly by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) does not indicate the feelings of the farmer representatives; at least it is not my own point of view. When we consider that the farmer's revenue has diminished to almost the vanishing point, so that he is scarcely able to make his living, a mere reduction of ten per cent in our sessional indemnity does not look very big to him. Indeed, I think the average agriculturist would suggest that we should be reduced considerably more than ten per cent.
So far as the wages are concerned, which the farmer pays to labour directly employed by him, they have been considerably reduced compared to what they were a few years ago; they have been reduced far more than ten per cent. It is only a matter of three or four years ago that the farmers were paying fifty and sixty dollars a month wages for the summer in my own district. This last year, or for the last two years in fact, they have been paying twenty, twenty-five and thirty dollars for the same work. The day wage a few years ago was five, six, seven and even eight dollars, whereas during the past two years it has been only a dollar and a half and two dollars.
The farmer cannot adopt the point of view which the labour representatives hold, of increasing wages in order to start a boom. He simply cannot do that; he has not the wherewithal to do it. Think of the young ladies and gentlemen engaged in the teaching profession. In the western country a few years

Those of us who live four or five days' journey from Ottawa, and some who live still farther away, find it quite expensive coming to this city and returning home. Those who live close to Ottawa, in Quebec or in Ontario, may not see this point quite so forcefully as those of us who live in the west or in the maritimes, but it costs us a good deal of money to travel.
Now, we are allowed an expense account for one trip down here and back, that is, supposing the session to start on a certain date and we continue in session until the business of the house is concluded, when we return home. There is nothing in that language to support the contention of the minister that I accused him, either inferentialiy or otherwise, of dismissing that lighthouse keeper. I may have said what I should not have said, but I think my hon. friend will agree that I was very careful in my statement in regard to this dismissal. However, the fact remains that a returned soldier was dismissed, and another man put in his place.
Before I sit down I should like to refer to one or two other matters which the Minister of Finance mentioned this afternoon. I want again of course to be careful in my language. When my hon. friend says, as he did this afternoon, that in Ottawa the civil servants were rather pleased or delighted that they did not receive a reduction of more than ten per cent and that this city was in a better position than any other city in Canada, he evidently is not quite in touch with conditions in Ottawa. There must be some reason for old Knox church being now the headquarters for the relief committee from the city. As the Ottawa newspapers stated yesterday, they are looking after four thousand families, the heads of which are out of employment. Surely if the heads of four thousand families in Ottawa are out of employment, the condition in this city is not as good as we would like it to be. Consequently, when my hon. friend says that Ottawa above all other cities can afford to take this ten per cent cut, he is not in touch with conditions here. Ottawa benefits more from the salaries of civil servants than does any other city in Canada. It is made up mostly of people in the employ of the government, and any reduction in their salaries has a detrimental effect upon the city. This is evident from the fact that in old Knox church a committee is at work looking after four thousand families the heads of which are out of employment. Consequently, I say again, as I said this afternoon, it is poor policy for this government to make a reduction of ten per cent in the salaries of civil servants or of anybody else.
What was the result last year? Is my hon. friend's position as Minister of Finance any

Salary Deduction Act
better than it was before the reduction took place last year? He was compelled then to come to the house with his budget in which, if my memoiy serves me rightly, as Minister of Finance he showed a deficit of some
350.000.	000. Is he in any better financial position to-day because of the fact that he has reduced the salaries of civil servants in Ottawa and, indeed, all over Canada? Oh, no, because even with that amount in the coffers of the government, I have no hesitation in saying that when the budget is brought down this year, instead of the deficit being $50,000,000, it will be almost double that amount. It is penny wise and pound foolish policy to reduce the earning power of our workers-because our civil servants are workers. What is the result of the government in their wisdom deciding to reduce the salaries of civil servants? Alm/ost every business firm in tine country said to its employees: We must reduce your wages; the government has set us the example; the government says that in order to carry on the
[DOT] affairs of the country, in order to balance the budget, it must reduce the salaries of civil servants all over this country by ten per cent, and we as business men must follow its lead and take ten per cent off your salaries. What has been the consequence? Not a saving of 32,000,000 or 33,000,000, which the government thought to save by this reduction, but throughout this country the purchasing power of the people has been reduced not
35.000.	000 but 350,000,000. I say to the Minister of Finance and to the government that it is poor, foolish policy to take ten per cent off the salaries of civil servants or anybody else if they are giving good value, because there is bound to be a reaction and this policy will have a bad effect in all parts of Canada. I appeal to my hon. friend, who is a reasonable man on most occasions. It is not good policy to make this reduction. What will it miean? It will mean a mere bagatelle in the affairs of the country. What difference does it make in his budget whether the deficit is
3100.000.	000 or 3102,000,000, especially when the 32,000,000 would be circulated from the Atlantic to the Pacific? My hon. friend can never save the country by this reduction of ten per cent, because as Minister of Finance he is setting a bad example to the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian National and every other business in Canada to reduce wages and consequently restrict the purchasing power of the people.
