I want to make a representation to the minister with regard to the blanket item of $200,000 for harbours and rivers generally, for maintenance of services, "no new works to be undertaken." As the minister probably knows, a very severe storm has swept the coast of Nova Scotia recently and it has done a great deal of damage to a number of small wharves and breakwaters there. Reports are coming to me and, I have no doubt, to the minister with regard to the matter. I was hoping that this vote could be so broadened that it might be possible for
essential work in the way of renewals to be undertaken-I am not speaking of neiw works. These small wharves and breakwaters are very essential in order that the fishing industry may be carried on. They provide shelter for the fishing boats and harbours which are not naturally available, and they make it possible for the fishermen to have their boats lie afloat so that they can go out at a comparatively reasonable hour instead of having to go out on the tide, as would be the ease if their boats were aground. It is not a matter of luxury but of absolute necessity; it is essential to the carrying on of their business. It affords employment and enables the fishermen through that to give assistance to the community. Does the minister consider this vote wide enough, assuming the amount were large enough, to undertake essential renewals of that kind in connection with small wharves and breakwaters seriously damaged by the storm?

I can understand my hon. friend's anxiety about this class of wharf, particularly in Nova Scotia where for the past two or three years there have been experiences similar to the one which he now relates. This vote is calculated to take care of just such improvements as he has mentioned, and the reference in the vote to the fact that no new works are to be undertaken means simply that we cannot start anything new, any new wharf out of the vote, but that it is intended to repair, rebuild or renew any existing structure, which I understand is what my hon. friend is urging. The report of the engineer comes in from time to time setting out the conditions and recommending those structures most in need of repair.

I may tell the minister that I addressed a letter to him to-day with reference to one particular structure, the partial demolition of which has come to my attention, a structure at the Hawk off Cape Sable island and another at Port La Tour where a part of the wharf has been rendered unusable. I want to commend these to the favourable consideration of the minister, and I shall bring to his attention others that are in need of repair.
Mr. STEM'ART (Leeds) : The whole of our vote last year was expended in this way and I am sure that this amount will not be found too large for our requirements. I shall certainly take my hon. friend's representations into very serious consideration.

I hope the vote will not be found too small.

I wish to add a word or two to what, the two previous speakers have said on this subject. On January 29 and 30 we had an unusually severe storm along the southeast coast of Nova Scotia, particularly affecting the constituency of my hon. friend from Shelbume-Yarmouth, the constituency of Halifax, the constituency of my hon. friend from Antigonish - Guysbocough and other points; and though I appreciate the fact that this vote of $200,000 is for ordinary expenses in connection with repairs, I would point out that there will be an unusually great demand for repairs owing to the destruction caused by the storm of the last two days of January. There are three letters of mine now in the mail addressed to the Minister of Public Works, directing his attention to three breakwaters and wharves in the county of Halifax which need attention, and I am sure others will be added to that list. I should like to say
a few words with regard to this vote covering public works in the province of Nova Scotia. I may say that times without number I have

interviewed the minister and I always found him sympathetic regarding my representations. I feel that he has done everything within reason to assist the fishermen in my constituency. I sympathize with the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough and the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth in the pleas they made for the fishermen of Nova Scotia, but I am rather sorry that hon. gentlemen opposite have not taken advantage of their position as members of the house to go to the minister to ask for estimates for their constituencies. If in making my plea I include the fishermen in the constituencies of Amti-gonieh-Guysborough and Shelbuimie-Yarmouth, I hope my hon. friends will mot hold it against me.
I am mot satisfied with the appropriations made for public works in the province of Nova Scotia. I may say to the minister that I do not hold anything against him personally; I have always found him willing to go out of his way to help the province of Nova Scotia, irrespective of political affiliations. But the fact remains that insufficient appropriations have been provided. The government is contributing direct relief, in many cases to people who do not deserve it, and consideration should be given to these fishermen. I am sure my hon. friends will agree that this matter should be kept entirely out of politics. Without wanting to criticize the minister personally, I may say that if some recognition is not given to the claims of these fishermen, this government or any other government is going to hear from me. I think in taking that stand I will have the support of my horn, friends opposite. I believe that in the constituency of Antigonish-Guysborough there are public works which should be provided, and I know that in my own constituency that is the case.
I should like to mention an instance at Broad Cove Marsh. Before giving the particulars, I may say that at the last election the vote in this district was about four to one in favour of my opponent. People in this district have never been in receipt of charity and they do not want charity; they would sooner jump into the sea and drown themselves. Because of inadequate public works these people are forced to go seven miles in order to land their fish. I will not stand for such a condition, whether it is a Conservative or a Liberal government in power.

Will you stand for the
results of the imperial conference?

I think my hon. friend said enough this afternoon. These people are descendants of old highland Scotch

Supply-Public Works-Harbours
people. They have never asked for charity; all they want is a chance to live. I intend to give them that chance. I realize the difficulty which the government is facing, but, to use a local expression, there is going to be blood on the moon if a wharf is not provided at Broad Cove Marsh. I do not care if I am read out of the party for taking this stand; I do not care what happens, I am going to see that these people who have never looked for charity, who would never take relief or anything, are given a chance to live. They are among the best citizens in the province, and at that many of them are Liberals. The chief engineer of the department was down there to look over the whole situation and his opinion was that a wharf should be provided. It is not provided for in the main estimates, and I am going to do my best to see that it is provided for in the supplementary estimates. Either that, or I am going to get out of politics.

Nothing doing. These people should be given a chance to earn their living, and I am not confining my remarks just to those in my own constituency.

But I am afraid that these estimates are not the right thing for the people of the province of Nova Scotia. I know the constituency of my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough probably as well as he does. I know that appropriations should be made to construct works to enable the fishermen in his county to carry on their vocation. If the government is prepared to give direct relief, not in all cases, but in some cases to bohunks, and in some cases to people who really do not deserve it, why should these old pioneers who have built up this country not be given at least a chance to live?

In reply to my hon. friend, who has made to me privately the representations he has made here tonight, I may say that with regard to Broad Cove Marsh we have had two or three wharves carried away. speechtext: I suggest that we confine the discussion to the item.

The item covers contributions to empire bureaux, and I suppose that they are a sort of clearing house for the farmer. I am discussing the exportation of farm products, but if this is not relevant I will not proceed. I have no desire to be disagreeable to the minister, but I think it my
duty as a member of this house to take up this matter which is of such vital importance to the farmer. As I said the other day, there are only two matters which are of interest to the people of Canada, unemployment and agriculture. I do not attach any blame to the government, I am only seeking information which will be satisfactory to the farmer. Last year some time, I forget whether it was in the first part of the year or the first part of our previous session, I asked a question on the orders of the day in connection with the imports of butter from either Australia or New Zealand. What are these bureaux and how much goes to each one?

When were these various bureaux founded and where are they located?
Mr. WEIR (Melfort. : I am sorry I have not that information before me.
Are they all located in London?
I believe they are all located in the United Kingdom with branches throughout the country, such as at Aberdeen.

In view of the lack of information available to the committee, I think that this item should stand. Surely the committee is not going to vote $21,000 as contributions to imperial bureaux when the
Supply-Agriculture

minister cannot tell us where they are. They may be located in South Africa, Australia, the Fiji islands, or even in Canada. We should have accurate information. Just where the information is gathered has no bearing upon the value of the work performed.

We do
not question that at all. Surely the committee is entitled to the information. We are asking the minister where the bureaux are located, what is their history and what they do. We should not be asked to vote $21,000 for an item which we do not understand and about which we are told nothing.

I believe this agreement was reached first in 1927 and was for a period of ten years. The centre of accumulation of information is, as I understand the matter, in London, but the information is gathered from various research bureaux, too numerous to mention, throughout the whole empire.

Do I
understand that the information that goes through this bureau goes through the Department of Agriculture, and if so, what officials in that department are responsible for cor-*elating the information?
Through the office of the deputy minister.

I do not understand why we should pay one cent to a research bureau situated outside Canada when we have a research bureau of our own where there are people who are just as competent as those who are in those bureaux the location of which the hon. gentleman does not know. In Ottawa on Sussex street, not far from here, there are competent men who do excellent work and in the minister's own department there are excellent cerealists and others who are experts in every branch of agriculture. There was Mr. Mackintosh, the discoverer of the famous apple. I do not see why we should make any contribution to a research bureau outside this country. We might subscribe to publications issued by bureaux that exist outside Canada, and I have no objection to that. We might occasionally have lectures from people who come from outside this country, but what interest have we in supporting these bureaux if they are of no benefit to us ? If the minister tells us what benefit those bureaux are to the Cana-[Mr. Vallance.J
dian farmer, perhaps I may reconsider my opinion in regard to the matter.

This money is
used not to support research laboratories in any part of the dominion, but as a means of setting up machinery to collect information as to discoveries that are made in various research laboratories throughout the empire so that we shall have the benefit of this without any expense to us other than this small amount.
Is that not what is done in this country? What are these people doing in our own research bureaux?

In our own research bureau they carry on certain research work. The result of that research work, when completed and thoroughly substantiated, will be sent to the central bureau, whence it will be disseminated to the various dominions so that they will be able to avail themselves of it without any expense other than that for the support of the bureau.
The minister has answered me very nicely. I reconsider my opinion.

I have no objection
to the $21,000 being voted. I realize, as the minister says, it is a very good thing for the various dominions and colonies of the empire to have a bureau such as this from which information may be disseminated to all other parts of the empire. The item " contributions to empire bureaux " explains itself, but still I think the minister should be able to say where the bureau is, whether it is in London, the seat of the empire. If there are several of them, we should know where they are. If they are all in the British Isles, I do not think that is good policy. Just as much research in certain lines is done in Canada as is done in the British Isles. Industrial research might be more expeditiously carried on in the British Isles, but so far as agriculture is concerned, we might at least expect to have a bureau located in Canada. We know we have our own dominion bureau. Now we have an empire bureau, and we should like to know where it is.

When this empire agreement was reached by the dominions, it was decided it would be advisable that the bureau be located in the United Kingdom. The agreement is for ten years, and during that period there would be ample time to bring the matter to the attention of the authorities if it were felt necessary at the end of that time to make a change.

We do not wish to be insistent, but we are within our rights. I would ask that the item stand.

I have no objection to the item standing, but so far as the bureau itself is concerned, I think we realize it is merely the machinery for collection and distribution of information, and it makes very little difference where it is located so long as the different dominions have agreed upon the point at which it would be located.
We have this empire bureau. Is there any one specific thing the minister can tell us that has been contributed from the bureau and that has not been developed by research in Canada?

One item to which they have made a great contribution and that we have not undertaken very extensively in this country has been carried on in the Rowett Institute at Aberdeen under Doctor Orr. It is perhaps the greatest work done in the world on nutrition, the uses, otherwise unknown, that can be made of very cheap feeds, such as potatoes and vegetables that otherwise would be wasted, and that the feeders in Scotland in olden times felt were of such little use that they considered they had to use much more expensive feeds.
Does the minister say that one of the bureaux is located in Aberdeen?
One of the research laboratories.
Has any Canadian been sent over there?
There is a Canadian now at the Rowett Institute. I think his name is Mackenzie.

I am not making an
effort to delay the committee, but it is through the questions we put to the minister
that the public is able to learn what is happening. That is the only way they have of obtaining knowledge as to why these moneys are voted. I say quite frankly that some of the actions of the government should be advertised, and this matter should be given all the publicity possible. For that reason I suggest that the item stand.

We may be asked by some of our constituents regarding this matter. I could not give them the information, because the minister has not been able to give it to us. I think it is reasonable to ask that the item stand, so that the information may be brought down later.

There is a report
covering a good many pages issued by these empire bureaux. If the committee so desires I shall bring down that report and read it from cover to cover, or lay it on the table. I suggest laying it on the table.
We are merely giving the minister an opportunity to open his department. Could not the item pass, and the minister bring in the information later on?

He has opened his department.
Item stands.

Mr. Chairman, I
ask you to call item No. 92.

Last night the Minister of Trade and Commerce advised the house as to the departments which would be gone into. At that time he did not mention the Department of National Defence, and I dc not think we ought to consider that department to-night.

If there is any opposition we shall not do so. The right hon. gentleman is quite correct; we did not name that department. The only reason I suggested it was that the Minister of Railways and Canals is ill-not seriously; he has a bad cold and had to go home. He has asked me if the committee will agree to calling an item in railways and canals, and as there are one or two noncontroversial items I think we might comply with his request. With that understanding I would ask the chairman to call item No. 99.
Department of Railways and Canals.
Miscellaneous-Printing and stationery, $7,000.
Would the minister give the details of this item?

Obviously the item is for the ordinary printing of the reports issued by

the Department of Railways and Canals from time to time. If it were necessary I think I could name a number of those reports; I am quite sure the hon. member is as familiar with them as I am. This vote provides for the ordinary printing necessary from year to year.

Is the
Duff report included?
No; I wish it were.
Item agreed to.

Would the right hon.
gentleman object to calling item No. 97, concerning the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada? I understand there could not be very great controversy in connection with this item.
Yes, there is.

I think that
item should be left for the attention of the minister.
How about item No. 101?
Leave the rest for the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals. Do not disappoint him.
Then, I can proceed only with my own department.
Go back to the Department of Agriculture,

If the right hon. gentleman. would be content to discuss that item in the Department of Agriculture estimates and pass it to-night, we might proceed. In the meantime however we shall turn to the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
The minister did not say anything about Trade and Commerce estimates yesterday.
They have been opened, of course.

The minister
intimated what estimates would be considered to-day, and he did not mention the Department of Trade and Commerce.
The right hon. gentleman is quite within his rights, if he insists upon them.
Some of the members would like to have a word concerning these estimates.

The house resumed from Friday, February 3, consideration in committee of Bill No. 19, to amend the Migratory Birds Convention Act-Mr. Murphy-Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
On section 2-R. C. M. police to be game officers.
I believe there was some information the minister wished to give in connection with this matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. G. MURPHY (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What information does the right hon. gentleman desire.

I had suggested to the Minister of Justice and to the minister in charge of the bill that this section 'be dropped, in view of the fact that already the minister has power to nominate members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police or anybody else, so far as that goes, for the purpose of carrying out the duties imposed under the act. The Minister of Justice said he would consider my suggestion. I had pointed out that in the province of Nova Scotia there would be about one hundred and sixty officers 'taking the place of nine or ten. Those one hundred and sixty officers would obviously have no particular knowledge regarding the matters in their care, whereas the nine or ten would understand the nature of the duties with which they were charged, and would have the technical information necessary to enable them properly to enforce the act. I understand very little about this subject, but I believe there is considerable to learn with regard to the habits of birds, and it seems to me that we would do well to have men well fitted for their work rather than by act of parliament provide a group of men who obviously are not acquainted with the duties they have to perform.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think the hon. member
is under a slight misapprehension in regard to these game officers. There was only one part of Canada in which they were appointed, and that is in the maritime provinces. In the western1 provinces we have one permanent officer m the person of Mr. Mumro. The game laws were enforced in those provinces, under the provincial acts and this dominion act, by the provincial police until their duties were taken over by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police under an arrangement made within the

Migratory Birds Convention Act
last year, I think, with the Department of Justice,, whereby the dominion police perform these duties. The same applied to Ontario and to the province of Quebec, with the exception of a small area along the river St. Lawrence. In the maritime provinces we had a permanent officer in the person of Mr. Tufts. Assisting him were five permanent officers known as assistant migratory bird officers, and there were additional men employed seasonally.
How many?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Possibly fifteen to twenty in the three provinces. These men were appointed seasonally, and were chosen from the localities in which the work was to be done. Now in place of employing those men seasonally it is proposed thait their duties be carried on by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. When the hon. member speaks of replacing nine or ten men with one hundred and fifty or one hundred and sixty he is in error. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police are on duty in those provinces now, and we are simply adding these duties to others which they already perform.

Perhaps I was under a
misapprehension, but that is not what I understood from the Minister of Justice. I understood from him that the idea was possibly to drop all these officers of which my hon. friend has spoken, at least all the assistants, and to substitute the full force of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, so that in effect the Migratory Birds Convention Act would be enforced under the direction of the Minister of Justice rather than the Minister of the Interior. From what my hon. friend just says it sounds to me that there is going to be Mr. Tufts, who is a very efficient officer, and I understand chief for the maritime provinces, the five officers of whom the minister has just spoken,, the five, I presume, permanent officers, the fifteen or twenty temporary officers to whom he referred, plus the number of mounted police there are in the maritime provinces; and speaking of Nova Scotia I think I am mot far wrong when I say there a,re about 150. The argument for this was that it was reducing expense. I cannot see that it is reducing expense if we are going to maintain the officers my hon. friend has already appointed and add let us say 150 who have no particular knowledge of the subject but who are members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am afraid I have not
made myself clear. These temporary men who have been appointed seasonally will not in future be appointed at all. Their duties 53719-121
will be performed by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Who have no experience.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Possibly some of the
temporary men appointed from year to year had not experience either.
Oh yes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend is more familiar-
May I point out that the men appointed in my district under the supervision of Mr. Lewis, who is a capable official, were nearly always the same men for five or six years, and their knowledge grows.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: New men were appointed from time to time. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police, being permanent officers and continuing in their duties from year to year, will become efficient men, because they will be continued in the job. May I point out that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have in recent years taken over the duties of the preventive service, which duties were formerly performed by officials or appointees of the Department of Inland Revenue.
That is a totally different sort of duty, more like police duties.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These men are to-day protecting the coasts of the maritime provinces from smuggling, they have their boats and are in a splendid position to protect the migratory birds from illegal shooting.

I do not exactly understand the minister's explanation. I understood the Minister of Justice the other evening to give an assurance to my hon. friend the member for Shelburne-Yarmouth that the government would consider specifying particular individuals among the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to whom would be delegated the duties assigned to them under this bill. I understand now that all the 150 or so mounted policemen in the maritimes will be potential game officers. That is exactly what we objected to the other day, and the Minister of Justice promised specifically that he would take this situation under advisement. I should like to know now from the Minister of the Interior what conclusion the administration has come to in regard to this question.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The former Section reads as follows:
5.	The minister may appoint game officers for. carrying out this act and the regulations, and may authorize such game officers to exercise the powers of a justice of the peace,-

1914	COMMONS
Migratory Birds Convention Act
It is that latter part with which the Minister of Justice was dealing when he said that such game officers might be designated for the exercise of the powers of justices of the peace, not that they would be appointed game officers. I hope my hon. friend follows me. We are proposing under this clause that all members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police shall for the purposes of this act be ex officio game officers. Under the old section the minister had the power to appoint game officers for the carrying out of the act. Action has already been taken transferring to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police the carrying out of the provisions of this act, in place of the Minister of the Interior appointing these officers seasonally. Then the further question arises as to whether the mounted police should exercise the powers of justices of the peace, and I agreed with the objection that was made, as expressed by the Minister of Justice, that it is not advisable that a prosecutor should also be a judge sitting on the case. I am very reliably informed that the mounted police themselves do not wish such authority, and do not exercise it when they can secure the services of a magistrate. I fail to see the objection which my hon. friend appears to urge against this clause.

The minister is quite correct in what he has stated, but in addition the Minister of Justice gave the assurance to which I refer, that he would consider, probably in collaboration with my hon. friend, whether the government would nominate specific officers to enforce the provisions of this act in the various provinces, or whether blanket authority would be given to members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police as such. I should like to know now the conclusion they arrived at in regard to the assurance that was given.

Let me refer the minister to Hansard, page 1775, to which my hon. friend the member for Vancouver Centre refers. I said:
But if the government are determined to have this work turned over to the mounted police, why not designate seven or eight or nine or ten officers who would have power to act, and not have 150 or 160 take the place of the nine men who are doing the work in Nova Scotia? That would obviate this blanketing in of the whole force, and you would be able to carry out exactly the same idea you have in mind if you want to transfer this work to the mounted police. Personally I think the idea is all wrong, and that the work should

remain -where it is, namely, under the responsible officers of the department which is administering the act.
And the Minister of Justice replied:
Mr. Guthrie: I am not at all wedded to the suggestion contained in the act, and if my hon. friend is serious in his suggestion I should be prepared to let this clause stand and discuss the matter with the officials of the mounted police. I think, however, there is a good deal to be said in favour of empowering all the members of the force to do particular acts or administer particular laws, and that is now done nr respect of other laws. ... If my hon. friend thinks there is merit in the suggestion that only a specific number be designated instead of the whole force, I am willing to consider it. I do not disfavour it at all. There is of course the principle that all members of the force should have equal powers. I will ask that the clause stand and we can discuss the matter further.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no desire to force the clause through in the absence of the Minister of Justice, nor have I any particular desire to have the clause passed in the bill. The minister has power under the present act to name every one of the 150 or 160 and therefore it can be done in any case even if this clause is dropped. If hon. members are very anxious that this clause should not carry we can at least let it stand, or I would be willing to drop it.

My point is that there could be much more efficient administration of the act by a specific naming of nine or ten men to do the work rather than, by act of parliament, blanketing the whole force. The Minister of Justice seemed to have the idea that he would be administering and appointing special men. He said at page 1774:
There may be points where at odd times it may be necessary to name some special officer's for a particular district for certain seasons of the year. I do not however anticipate that will be necessary.
Mr. Ralston: What minister will do that?
Mr. Guthrie: That will be the mounted police.
It sounded to me therefore as if the mounted police were taking the place entirely of the officers to whom the minister referred earlier this evening.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is not a correct interpretation of the situation, because the minister designated to carry out the act is the Minister of the Interior and therefore that responsibility devolves upon him. However-

That was not the impression we got the other day. We

Questions
distinctly got the impression that this was another step in the progressive dismemberment of the Department of the Interior and that all these powers would be vested in the Minister of Justice. Now the minister says that it will rest with the Department of the Interior. I should like to let it stand until the Minister of Justice is here so that we shall know just where we are.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Very well.
Progress reported.
